summary: The note is an incident report on how Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs) and the geomagnetic storms they trigger can disrupt undersea cable networks by inducing currents in the cables' conductive copper sheathing. It uses the September 15, 2023 CME event (K-index 7) as a case study, describing latency issues, data errors, and overheating damage on transoceanic routes. It closes with mitigation measures: better space weather forecasting, improved cable design and voltage stabilization, collaboration, and operational training.
one_line: Report on how the September 2023 coronal mass ejection induced currents in undersea cables, causing disruptions, and how operators can mitigate such space weather risks.
key_facts: A Coronal Mass Ejection (CME) is a significant release of plasma and magnetic field from the solar corona, often associated with solar flares and sunspot activity.
Earth-directed CMEs travel at 250 to over 2,000 kilometers per second and typically arrive within one to five days after eruption.
Geoeffectiveness of a CME depends largely on its speed, direction, and the orientation of its embedded magnetic fields as it interacts with Earth's magnetosphere.
Geomagnetic storms induce geomagnetic induced currents (GICs) in conductive structures such as pipelines, power grids, and undersea cable networks.
As of September 2023, hundreds of active undersea cables with a combined length of over 1.3 million kilometers carry 98% of all international internet traffic.

Induced currents flow in the copper sheathing used in fiberoptic undersea cables for power and grounding; they are negligible normally but can become significantly stronger during a geomagnetic storm.
On September 15, 2023, a strong CME struck Earth, producing a K-index of 7; storms of this magnitude occur roughly 60 times per solar cycle, or once every 11 years, according to the note.
Dr. Emily Rodriguez of the National Space Weather Program called the event 'a classic example of a Carrington-level event,' though not as severe as the one in 1859.
After the September 2023 CME, telecom companies reported latency issues and data transmission errors on several transoceanic routes.
Interconnect Telecom's trans-Pacific cable was among the hardest hit; CEO John Abrams said induced current activated built-in protection, causing several hours of managed downtime.
Damage assessments found localized overheating in cable sections from current surges, leaving them inoperable until repair crews replaced the affected segments.

Proposed mitigations include better CME arrival and strength forecasting, rerouting traffic or shutting down vulnerable segments, more shielding and grounding, fiber less susceptible to induction, and wider use of voltage-stabilizing equipment.
The note also recommends inter-agency and cross-sector data sharing, standardized response protocols, and regular training exercises simulating severe space weather.
